result.title: The relationship between sleep quality and academic performance among university students.
result.content:
This paper synthesizes published evidence to examine the relationship between sleep quality and academic performance among university students, drawing upon 30 source records. The review reveals a complex and often inconsistent picture: while a substantial body of literature indicates that poor sleep quality and insufficient sleep duration negatively affect academic outcomes across various global contexts, other research has found no significant association. Intriguingly, some studies even report a positive correlation between poorer sleep and higher academic achievement in specific circumstances.

The principal themes emerging from the literature include the prevalence of poor sleep quality among university students and its association with lower academic performance, impaired cognitive functions (such as attention, working memory, and executive function), and increased stress and emotional fatigue. However, conflicting findings suggest the influence of moderating factors, such as academic demands, individual coping strategies, gender differences, and lifestyle choices.

A key limitation highlighted is the extreme heterogeneity across studies, which complicates drawing definitive conclusions, as evidenced by a meta-analysis identifying a non-significant small positive pooled correlation. The synthesis also points to a need for more research that systematically investigates underlying mediating or moderating factors and for longitudinal studies to understand the evolving nature of these relationships over time. Overall, the evidence suggests that promoting healthy sleep habits and stress management could enhance student well-being and academic achievement, though the precise nature of the sleep-performance link remains nuanced.

The transition to university represents a period of significant change for students, encompassing maturational, psychosocial, and academic adjustments that can influence various aspects of their well-being, including sleep patterns [S1][S7]. Academic achievement is critical for student retention and long-term success [S4], and sleep is increasingly recognized as a modifiable determinant of academic performance [S4]. University students frequently report insufficient or poor quality sleep, which has been linked to negative academic outcomes [S1][S7][S10][S21][S27]. This issue is particularly pronounced during periods of high academic demand, such as examination periods [S1].

Multiple studies have investigated the relationship between sleep quality and academic performance, often employing the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) to assess sleep [S3][S8][S11][S12][S13][S14]. Research across various contexts, including Spain [S1][S7], Saudi Arabia [S2][S13][S18], New Zealand [S3], the United States [S5][S20][S28], Rwanda [S6], Nigeria [S8][S10][S11], Malaysia [S9][S15], Sri Lanka [S12], and Pakistan [S16][S21], consistently suggests that inadequate sleep negatively affects academic performance [S7]. Specifically, shorter sleep duration, often below 6-7 hours per night, has been associated with poorer academic achievement [S4][S19][S28]. Poor sleep quality has also been linked to lower academic performance in several studies [S4][S5][S6][S8][S12][S14][S27][S29]. For instance, students with good sleep quality have demonstrated significantly higher academic performance scores compared to those with poor sleep quality [S6][S8][S12][S27]. Conversely, some studies have reported no significant relationship between sleep quality and academic performance [S2][S3][S13][S24][S25]. Notably, a positive correlation between poor sleep and better academic performance has also been observed, with some findings suggesting that longer waking hours for academic commitments might be perceived as beneficial for grades in later years of study [S9][S15]. These divergent findings underscore the complexity of this relationship and the potential influence of contextual and individual factors.

While the existing literature highlights a general association between sleep quality and academic performance, a meta-analysis on this topic identified a non-significant small positive pooled correlation, with extreme heterogeneity among studies [S20]. This heterogeneity suggests that the relationship may be influenced by various mediating or moderating factors that require further exploration. Moreover, some studies have focused on specific student populations, such as first-year students [S3][S4][S5] or health sciences students [S2][S6][S14], and have examined various aspects of sleep, including duration, quality, chronotype, and sleep disorders [S4][S7]. However, there remains a need to synthesize findings across diverse populations and methodologies to better understand the nuances of this relationship.

This paper will synthesize published evidence to examine the relationship between sleep quality and academic performance among university students, drawing upon the available literature.

This paper presents a narrative synthesis of the evidence available to the writing run for the stated research question. The run assembled 30 distinct source records from OpenAlex. This is the available source pool, not the number of studies ultimately cited or a count from a systematic screening process. The synthesis draws on the metadata and source excerpts supplied by those records; access to every full text is not assumed. It compares reported relationships, differences in study contexts and methods, and limitations relevant to the research question. Search strategy: sources were retrieved on 30 October 2026 using the queries "The relationship between sleep quality and academic performance among university students.". Automated topical screening (term matching on titles and abstracts, not reading of full texts) found the core concepts in this many of the 30 records: "sleep quality" in 30, "academic performance" in 30. No study-design, sample or date inclusion criteria were applied beyond this topical screening. This is not an exhaustive or systematic review: no predefined screening protocol, independent double screening, comprehensive search coverage, or formal risk-of-bias assessment is claimed. Source identity checks and claim-support checks are separate, and remaining uncertainties are retained as review flags. No original participants were recruited, new dataset collected, or original statistical analysis performed for this literature-based paper.

The available literature suggests a complex and often inconsistent relationship between sleep quality and academic performance among university students, with some studies indicating a negative association, others reporting no significant link, and a few even noting a positive correlation between poorer sleep and better academic outcomes in specific contexts [S2][S3][S9][S13][S15][S24][S25]. This heterogeneity is highlighted by a meta-analysis, which identified a non-significant small positive pooled correlation between sleep quality and academic achievement, along with extreme variability across studies [S20].

### Negative Associations Between Poor Sleep and Academic Performance

A substantial body of research indicates that poor sleep quality and insufficient sleep duration are detrimental to academic success [S1][S4][S6][S7][S8][S10][S11][S12][S14][S18][S19][S21][S27][S28][S29]. Studies from diverse geographical locations, including Spain [S1][S7], Rwanda [S6], Nigeria [S8][S10][S11], Sri Lanka [S12], Pakistan [S21], Saudi Arabia [S18], and the United States [S5][S28], have reported that students experiencing poor sleep quality or deprivation tend to exhibit lower academic performance. For example, students with good sleep quality in Rwanda and Nigeria demonstrated significantly higher academic performance scores compared to those with poor sleep quality [S6][S8]. Similarly, a study in Spain found a positive association between sleep quality and academic performance during examination periods, noting that insufficient and poor-quality sleep negatively affected performance [S1]. In Sri Lanka, better sleep patterns, including duration and subjective sleep quality, were associated with higher academic performance [S12].

Specific aspects of sleep, such as duration, have also been linked to academic outcomes. Shorter sleep duration, often below 6-7 hours per night, is generally associated with poorer academic achievement [S4][S19][S28]. A Japanese study found that students with worse grades reported significantly shorter sleep durations [S19]. Moreover, poor overall sleep quality has been strongly correlated with lower academic performance [S6][S14][S27][S29]. This negative impact extends to cognitive functions essential for academic work, with sleep deprivation significantly impairing attention, working memory, processing speed, and executive function in college students [S21][S28]. Poor sleepers often have lower cognitive scores across all domains compared to good sleepers, especially under academic stress [S21]. Additionally, later bedtimes have been associated with lower academic performance in first-year university students [S3].

Beyond direct academic metrics, poor sleep quality is often associated with factors that indirectly affect academic performance. High perceived stress levels are linked to both poor sleep quality and lower cognitive performance [S11][S21][S23]. Poor sleep quality increases emotional fatigue, which in turn reduces academic performance [S29]. The prevalence of poor sleep quality among university students is a widespread concern, with many studies reporting a significant proportion of students experiencing it [S1][S6][S8][S9][S11][S17][S18][S21][S23][S27]. Factors such as social media addiction have also been identified as predictors of very poor sleep quality [S17].

### Absence or Positive Associations

While many studies point to a negative relationship, some research has reported no significant association between sleep quality and academic performance [S2][S3][S13][S24][S25]. For instance, a study of health sciences students in Saudi Arabia found no significant difference between sleep quality and GPA, although it did note that students sleeping 6 to 7 hours performed better academically than those sleeping less [S2][S13]. A New Zealand study of first-year students also found no significant differences in academic performance between students with poor, moderate, and good sleep quality, though later bedtimes were associated with lower performance [S3]. Similarly, studies in Malaysia [S24] and India [S25] found no significant relationship between sleep quality and academic achievement or self-control's impact on it.

Intriguingly, some studies suggest a positive correlation between poor sleep and better academic performance in certain circumstances [S9][S15]. In Malaysia, one study found that poor sleep was associated with better academic performance, and that students who were "poor-sleepers" were more likely to have higher academic achievement in later years of study [S9]. Another Malaysian study similarly suggested that "poor-sleepers" had higher academic achievement in senior years, implying that longer waking hours for academic commitments might be perceived as beneficial for grades [S15]. These findings introduce nuance, suggesting that the relationship is not always straightforward and may be influenced by factors such as academic demands and student coping strategies.

### Moderating Factors and Contextual Influences

The varied findings underscore the influence of moderating or mediating factors. Affective factors can influence the relationship between sleep quality and academic performance [S4]. Gender differences have been observed, with female students often reporting worse sleep quality and a higher frequency of nightmares compared to male students, and female students generally reporting slightly better sleep quality but poorer academic performance compared to their male counterparts in some contexts [S6][S13][S26][S27]. Conversely, in a Rwandan study, male gender was correlated with higher academic scores [S6]. Socioeconomic status and specific student populations (e.g., first-year students, health sciences students) can also play a role [S3][S4][S5][S6][S14].

Lifestyle factors such as screen time and caffeine intake have been linked to sleep quality and duration [S22][S2

The published literature presents a multifaceted and often contradictory picture of the relationship between sleep quality and academic performance among university students. While a prevalent view suggests that poor sleep negatively impacts academic outcomes, a notable proportion of studies report no significant association, and some even indicate a positive correlation between poorer sleep and higher academic achievement in specific contexts [S2][S3][S9][S13][S15][S24][S25]. This marked heterogeneity is underscored by a meta-analysis, which found a non-significant small positive pooled correlation between sleep quality and academic achievement, along with extreme variability across the studies included in that analysis [S20].

A significant body of research points to a negative relationship, asserting that inadequate sleep quality and duration are detrimental to academic success [S1][S4][S6][S7][S8][S10][S11][S12][S14][S18][S19][S21][S27][S28][S29]. Studies from various countries, including Spain [S1][S7], Rwanda [S6], Nigeria [S8][S10][S11], Sri Lanka [S12], Pakistan [S21], Saudi Arabia [S18], and the United States [S5][S28], consistently indicate that students experiencing poor sleep quality or deprivation tend to exhibit lower academic performance. For example, students with good sleep quality in Rwanda and Nigeria were found to have significantly higher academic performance scores than those with poor sleep quality [S6][S8]. Similarly, a study in Spain observed a positive association between sleep quality and academic performance during examination periods, noting that insufficient and poor-quality sleep adversely affected performance [S1]. In Sri Lanka, better sleep patterns, encompassing both duration and subjective quality, correlated with higher academic performance [S12]. Shorter sleep duration, often defined as less than 6-7 hours per night, is commonly associated with poorer academic achievement [S4][S19][S28]. A Japanese study reported that students with lower grades generally had significantly shorter sleep durations [S19]. Furthermore, poor overall sleep quality has been strongly correlated with lower academic performance [S6][S14][S27][S29], and sleep deprivation can impair cognitive functions vital for academic work, such as attention, working memory, processing speed, and executive function [S21][S28]. Poor sleepers have demonstrated lower cognitive scores across all domains, particularly under academic stress [S21]. Later bedtimes have also been linked to lower academic performance among first-year university students [S3].

Conversely, several studies contradict this prevailing negative association. Some research has reported no significant relationship between sleep quality and academic performance [S2][S3][S13][S24][S25]. For instance, a study involving health sciences students in Saudi Arabia found no significant difference between sleep quality and GPA, though it did note that students sleeping 6 to 7 hours performed better academically than those sleeping less [S2][S13]. A New Zealand study of first-year students similarly found no significant differences in academic performance across varying sleep quality levels, despite observing an association between later bedtimes and lower performance [S3]. Malaysian [S24] and Indian [S25] studies also reported no significant link between sleep quality and academic achievement.

Intriguingly, a few studies present findings that suggest a positive correlation between poor sleep and better academic performance in specific contexts [S9][S15]. In Malaysia, one study indicated that poor sleep was associated with better academic performance, with "poor-sleepers" being more likely to achieve higher academic success in later years of study [S9]. Another Malaysian study similarly suggested that "poor-sleepers" achieved higher academic results in senior years, proposing that longer waking hours dedicated to academic commitments might be perceived as beneficial for grades [S15]. These findings introduce a significant nuance, challenging the straightforward assumption that all instances of poor sleep are detrimental to academic outcomes and implying that the relationship may be mediated by individual coping strategies or academic demands.

The inconsistencies across studies highlight the potential influence of moderating or mediating factors. Affective factors can play a role in the relationship between sleep quality and academic performance [S4]. Gender differences have been observed, with female students often reporting worse sleep quality and a higher frequency of nightmares compared to male students [S27]. However, findings on gender and academic performance are mixed; some studies report females having slightly better sleep quality but poorer academic performance compared to males [S26][S27], while a Rwandan study found male gender to be correlated with higher academic scores [S6]. Socioeconomic status and specific student populations, such as first-year students [S3][S4][S5] or health sciences students [S2][S6][S14], may also influence these relationships. Lifestyle factors, including screen time and caffeine intake, have been linked to sleep quality and duration [S22][S26]. High perceived stress levels are consistently associated with both poor sleep quality and lower cognitive performance [S11][S21][S23]. Poor sleep quality has also been linked to increased emotional fatigue, which, in turn, reduces academic performance [S29]. The prevalence of poor sleep quality among university students is a widespread concern, reported in numerous studies across different regions

The literature reviewed reveals several research gaps in understanding the relationship between sleep quality and academic performance among university students. The primary gap stems from the inconsistent and sometimes contradictory findings across existing studies [S2][S3][S9][S13][S15][S20][S24][S25]. A meta-analysis identified a non-significant small positive pooled correlation with extreme heterogeneity, suggesting that unexamined mediating or moderating factors significantly influence this relationship [S20]. While some studies link poor sleep to lower performance, others find no association, or even a positive correlation between poor sleep and higher grades in specific contexts [S2][S3][S9][S13][S15][S24][S25]. This highlights a need for research that systematically investigates these underlying factors.

Specifically, the nuanced influence of academic demands and student coping strategies on the sleep-performance relationship remains underexplored. Some Malaysian studies suggest that "poor-sleepers" might achieve higher academic success in later years, implying that longer waking hours for academic commitments could be perceived as beneficial [S9][S15]. This challenges the general assumption that all poor sleep is detrimental and indicates a gap in understanding how students strategically manage sleep amidst academic pressures and how these strategies impact outcomes.

Furthermore, while several studies note the prevalence of poor sleep quality among university students across diverse regions [S1][S6][S8][S9][S11][S17][S18][S21][S23][S27], there is limited synthesis of these findings to identify common, cross-cultural predictors or consequences of poor sleep in this population. The literature also notes that specific components of sleep, such as chronotype and sleep disorders, have been examined [S4][S7], but a comprehensive synthesis across these diverse aspects of sleep and their varied impacts on academic performance is still needed. Longitudinal studies are explicitly recommended to better understand the direction and nature of these complex relationships over time [S6][S12].

The available literature presents a complex and at times contradictory view of the relationship between sleep quality and academic performance in university students. While a substantial number of studies indicate that poor sleep quality and insufficient sleep duration negatively affect academic outcomes across various global contexts, other research has found no significant association, or, in some specific cases, a positive correlation between poorer sleep and higher academic achievement. This heterogeneity is further highlighted by a meta-analysis that reported a non-significant small positive pooled correlation with extreme variability among studies, suggesting that the relationship is influenced by numerous unexamined mediating or moderating factors.

Many studies confirm that poor sleep quality, often characterized by shorter sleep duration (below 6-7 hours per night), is associated with lower academic performance and impaired cognitive functions essential for academic success, such as attention, working memory, processing speed, and executive function. Additionally, factors like perceived stress, emotional fatigue, later bedtimes, and lifestyle choices such as screen time and caffeine intake are linked to poorer sleep quality and, consequently, to reduced academic performance.

However, the instances where no clear link, or even a positive one, was observed between poor sleep and academic success, particularly in some Malaysian studies suggesting that longer waking hours for academic commitments might be perceived as beneficial, emphasize the need for a more nuanced understanding. Future research should systematically investigate the influence of academic demands and student coping strategies on this relationship. Longitudinal studies will also be crucial for understanding the direction and evolving nature of these complex interactions over time. Such research could inform university strategies aimed at promoting healthy sleep habits and stress management to enhance student well-being and academic achievement.

While a substantial number of studies indicate that poor sleep quality and insufficient sleep duration negatively affect academic outcomes across various global contexts, other research has found no significant association, or, in some specific cases, a positive correlation between poorer sleep and higher academic achievement. researchPaperSectionResults.heading: Abstract
researchPaperSectionResults.content:
This paper synthesizes published evidence to examine the relationship between sleep quality and academic performance among university students, drawing upon 30 source records. The review reveals a complex and often inconsistent picture: while a substantial body of literature indicates that poor sleep quality and insufficient sleep duration negatively affect academic outcomes across various global contexts, other research has found no significant association. Intriguingly, some studies even report a positive correlation between poorer sleep and higher academic achievement in specific circumstances.

The principal themes emerging from the literature include the prevalence of poor sleep quality among university students and its association with lower academic performance, impaired cognitive functions (such as attention, working memory, and executive function), and increased stress and emotional fatigue. However, conflicting findings suggest the influence of moderating factors, such as academic demands, individual coping strategies, gender differences, and lifestyle choices.

A key limitation highlighted is the extreme heterogeneity across studies, which complicates drawing definitive conclusions, as evidenced by a meta-analysis identifying a non-significant small positive pooled correlation. The synthesis also points to a need for more research that systematically investigates underlying mediating or moderating factors and for longitudinal studies to understand the evolving nature of these relationships over time. Overall, the evidence suggests that promoting healthy sleep habits and stress management could enhance student well-being and academic achievement, though the precise nature of the sleep-performance link remains nuanced.

researchPaperSectionResults.heading: Introduction
researchPaperSectionResults.content:
The transition to university represents a period of significant change for students, encompassing maturational, psychosocial, and academic adjustments that can influence various aspects of their well-being, including sleep patterns [S1][S7]. Academic achievement is critical for student retention and long-term success [S4], and sleep is increasingly recognized as a modifiable determinant of academic performance [S4]. University students frequently report insufficient or poor quality sleep, which has been linked to negative academic outcomes [S1][S7][S10][S21][S27]. This issue is particularly pronounced during periods of high academic demand, such as examination periods [S1].

Multiple studies have investigated the relationship between sleep quality and academic performance, often employing the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) to assess sleep [S3][S8][S11][S12][S13][S14]. Research across various contexts, including Spain [S1][S7], Saudi Arabia [S2][S13][S18], New Zealand [S3], the United States [S5][S20][S28], Rwanda [S6], Nigeria [S8][S10][S11], Malaysia [S9][S15], Sri Lanka [S12], and Pakistan [S16][S21], consistently suggests that inadequate sleep negatively affects academic performance [S7]. Specifically, shorter sleep duration, often below 6-7 hours per night, has been associated with poorer academic achievement [S4][S19][S28]. Poor sleep quality has also been linked to lower academic performance in several studies [S4][S5][S6][S8][S12][S14][S27][S29]. For instance, students with good sleep quality have demonstrated significantly higher academic performance scores compared to those with poor sleep quality [S6][S8][S12][S27]. Conversely, some studies have reported no significant relationship between sleep quality and academic performance [S2][S3][S13][S24][S25]. Notably, a positive correlation between poor sleep and better academic performance has also been observed, with some findings suggesting that longer waking hours for academic commitments might be perceived as beneficial for grades in later years of study [S9][S15]. These divergent findings underscore the complexity of this relationship and the potential influence of contextual and individual factors.

While the existing literature highlights a general association between sleep quality and academic performance, a meta-analysis on this topic identified a non-significant small positive pooled correlation, with extreme heterogeneity among studies [S20]. This heterogeneity suggests that the relationship may be influenced by various mediating or moderating factors that require further exploration. Moreover, some studies have focused on specific student populations, such as first-year students [S3][S4][S5] or health sciences students [S2][S6][S14], and have examined various aspects of sleep, including duration, quality, chronotype, and sleep disorders [S4][S7]. However, there remains a need to synthesize findings across diverse populations and methodologies to better understand the nuances of this relationship.

This paper will synthesize published evidence to examine the relationship between sleep quality and academic performance among university students, drawing upon the available literature.

researchPaperSectionResults.heading: Research Gaps
researchPaperSectionResults.content:
The literature reviewed reveals several research gaps in understanding the relationship between sleep quality and academic performance among university students. The primary gap stems from the inconsistent and sometimes contradictory findings across existing studies [S2][S3][S9][S13][S15][S20][S24][S25]. A meta-analysis identified a non-significant small positive pooled correlation with extreme heterogeneity, suggesting that unexamined mediating or moderating factors significantly influence this relationship [S20]. While some studies link poor sleep to lower performance, others find no association, or even a positive correlation between poor sleep and higher grades in specific contexts [S2][S3][S9][S13][S15][S24][S25]. This highlights a need for research that systematically investigates these underlying factors.

Specifically, the nuanced influence of academic demands and student coping strategies on the sleep-performance relationship remains underexplored. Some Malaysian studies suggest that "poor-sleepers" might achieve higher academic success in later years, implying that longer waking hours for academic commitments could be perceived as beneficial [S9][S15]. This challenges the general assumption that all poor sleep is detrimental and indicates a gap in understanding how students strategically manage sleep amidst academic pressures and how these strategies impact outcomes.

Furthermore, while several studies note the prevalence of poor sleep quality among university students across diverse regions [S1][S6][S8][S9][S11][S17][S18][S21][S23][S27], there is limited synthesis of these findings to identify common, cross-cultural predictors or consequences of poor sleep in this population. The literature also notes that specific components of sleep, such as chronotype and sleep disorders, have been examined [S4][S7], but a comprehensive synthesis across these diverse aspects of sleep and their varied impacts on academic performance is still needed. Longitudinal studies are explicitly recommended to better understand the direction and nature of these complex relationships over time [S6][S12].
